lesson.title: Dauer & Termin: der Moment, dauern, der Termin, die Sekunde, das Datum
lesson.subtitle: how long things last — and the Latin hiding inside the most German verb in the room

hook.title: Even the Waiting Is Roman
hook.content: You already say when (jetzt, sofort, später) and how often (oft, einmal). Today: how LONG. Der Moment is Latin momentum, 'movement' — a moment is one beat of the moving world, and English momentum in physics class is the same word in a lab coat. Der Termin is Latin terminus, the boundary stone a Roman planted where his land ended — a Termin is an end-point planted in your day, and English terminus and terminal are the same stone. Die Sekunde is Latin secundus, 'the following' — the minute's follower, sixty of them deep; English second is the same follower. Das Datum is Latin datum, 'the given' — the date is what the calendar hands you, and English data is literally the same word in the plural. And the sleeper: dauern looks like the most German verb alive, but it walked in from Latin durare, 'to last, to hold out' — dauern and English during, duration, durable are one verb in two coats.

footnotes.title: The Politeness Pair
footnotes.content: Einen Moment, bitte and Eine Sekunde, bitte are the two standard 'one moment, please's — accusative, because the moment is the thing you are being handed. Moment buys you patience; Sekunde buys you urgency. Same frame, different clock.

pattern.title: Dauern Eats the Accusative
pattern.content: One frame carries the lesson: Der Termin dauert zwanzig Minuten — the duration stands in the accusative with NO preposition, exactly like Ich warte zehn Minuten. The question is just the frame tilted: Wie lange dauert der Termin? The politeness pair rides the same accusative: Einen Moment, bitte! Eine Sekunde, bitte! The scale climbs — die Sekunde, die Minute, die Stunde — and the case never changes. And the date: Wie ist das Datum heute? — Heute ist der 3. Oktober. Zero fits the same clock: Es ist null Uhr — Mitternacht.
pattern.linguist_note: The accusative of duration is inherited, not invented: Latin measured time the same bare way (multos annos, 'for many years' — accusative, no preposition). German's dauern kept the old measurement; English needs a 'for' and moves on.

exercises.prompt: Moments, seconds, appointments — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The appointment is early in the morning
matching_pairs.german: Der Termin ist früh am Morgen

exercises.target_answer: Einen Moment, bitte, Eine Sekunde, bitte, Der Termin dauert zwanzig Minuten, Null ist eine Zahl, Eine Million hat sechs Nullen, Der Termin ist früh am Morgen, Bis später
exercises.meaning: the politeness pair, the duration frame, and the numbers on the clock
exercises.explanation: The accusative is everywhere: einen Moment (der Moment), eine Sekunde (die Sekunde), zwanzig Minuten — duration and objects, no preposition in sight. And the numbers you drilled are already inside: null, eine Million, sechs Nullen.

exercises.prompt: 'Der Termin dauert zwanzig Minuten.' What case is 'zwanzig Minuten' — and what does that tell you about dauern?
exercises.meaning: dauern takes a bare accusative of duration
exercises.explanation: dauern measures its span with a bare accusative — zwanzig Minuten, keine Präposition. It is the same measurement as Ich warte zehn Minuten, and the same construction Latin used: the duration simply stands there, unmarked.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the duration question: 'How long does the appointment last'
exercises.meaning: How long does the appointment last?

vocab_hints.note: Wie lange asks about DURATION — how long it lasts, from start to finish.

exercises.explanation: Wie lange dauert ...? is the all-purpose duration question — swap the subject and it still works: Wie lange dauert der Kaffee, die Stunde, der Winter? The verb dauert sits in slot 2, as always.

exercises.prompt: 'Das Datum' is Latin datum, 'the given'. Which English word is that same Latin word in the plural — the one you type every day?
exercises.meaning: Datum ↔ data: one Latin participle, two languages
exercises.explanation: Datum is the neuter past participle of Latin dare, 'to give' — 'the given'. English data is literally that same word in the plural, and English date came through the same medieval Latin channel. The calendar hands you data every time you write a Datum.
Jetzt takes position 1, habe slides to slot 2 — the V2 swap from the time-adverb lesson. einen Termin is masculine accusative, the same case as einen Moment, bitte.

summary.outcome: Say how long something lasts with dauern + bare accusative, book a Termin, ask the date, and buy patience with Einen Moment, bitte.

use_example.german: Wie lange dauert der Termin? — Zwanzig Minuten.
use_example.english: How long does the appointment last? — Twenty minutes.

summary.takeaway: Moment, Termin, Sekunde, Datum are Latin loans — and so, in disguise, is dauern (durare ↔ during). Duration takes a bare accusative: Der Termin dauert zwanzig Minuten.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Ort I — hier, dort, drüben, gegenüber, der Umweg — the words that tell you where.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Dauer & Termin: der Moment, dauern, der Termin, die Sekunde, das Datum (Now I have an appointment):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Jetzt habe ich einen Termin" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Dauer & Termin: der Moment, dauern, der Termin, die Sekunde, das Datum without relying on short-term echo.

moment.etymology_derivation: From Latin momentum — the same Latin loan as English moment. [wiktionary]

dauern.etymology_derivation: From Latin dūrō via Middle Low German — kin to archaic English dure, as in endure. [wiktionary]

termin.context_phrase: Ich habe morgen einen Termin beim Zahnarzt.
termin.context_translation: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow.
termin.etymology_derivation: From Latin terminus, boundary or limit — the same Latin word that gives English term and terminus. [wiktionary]

sekunde.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin secunda, short for pars minuta secunda, the second small part of the hour — the same Latin phrase behind English second. [wiktionary]

datum.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin datum, literally something given — the same Latin participle that gave English date, from the Roman letter formula given at Rome. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

stunde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stundu — cognate with archaic English stound 'hour'. [wiktionary]

null.etymology_derivation: From Italian nulla, Latin nullus 'none' — the same Latin loan as English null. [wiktionary]

zahl.context_phrase: Die Zahl sieben ist meine Glückszahl.
zahl.context_translation: The number seven is my lucky number.
zahl.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *talō — the entry lists English tale as a cognate, the same tal-root as tell; the initial t became z. [wiktionary]

million.context_phrase: Die Stadt hat eine Million Menschen.
million.context_translation: The city has one million people.
million.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian millione — the same Italian loan as English million. [wiktionary]

jetzt.etymology_derivation: Old High German iozuo, je (ever) + zu (to); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

später.etymology_derivation: Comparative of spät (late); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

früh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī); only Dutch/Low German cognates listed. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

elektriker.etymology_derivation: elektrisch (electric) + -er; elektrisch is from Neo-Latin electricus, coined by William Gilbert from Greek elektron (amber) - the stone where static electricity was first noticed; English electric is the same coinage. [wiktionary][etymonline]

sonnenbrille.context_phrase: Im Sommer brauche ich die Sonnenbrille.
sonnenbrille.context_translation: In summer I need the sunglasses.
sonnenbrille.etymology_derivation: Sonne + -n- + Brille, the exact mirror of sunglasses: Sonne is the documented twin of sun, and Brille is the dictionary's glasses-word. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
